I might go further and tell the hon. gentleman that I have been connected with the cheese trade for thirty years in the county of Oxford, and, until of late years, at any rate, very few of the factories bought milk from the patrons in that county. The reason given for this bonus was to induce the people to put in cold storage chambers. Alost of them felt it was too much of an expense for the factory to put it in, as it would cost a couple of hundred dollars. As a matter of fact, these cold storage chambers were not put in until this measure was brought in and this assistance given.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Can the bon. gentleman tell whether Mr. Macpherson or the farmers own the factories ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Mr. Macpherson owns them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That explains it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
There are dozens of these factories that do not belong to Mr. Macpherson, though he happens to own a great many of them. Take Mr. Macleod, for instance ; or the Lome factories-I could mention them by the dozens, and every one of them coming under this bonus, if they applied for it under the Act. I only desired to point out that the hon. gentleman wanted to take a fling at Mr. Macpherson, instead of giving credit to the government for trying to assist the farmers.
To promote dairying interests by advances lor milk and cream, and for making butter and cheese, to be recouped out of the proceeds of sales of such butter and cheese, to be placed to the credit of the consolidated revenue fund, $60,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I suppose the committee understands that this item is for advances which were made to the farmers on their creamery accounts until the butter is actually sold, and the advances are then recouped out of the proceeds of the sales. The creameries in tne North-west have been managed by the department now for four years. I think I may say the industry in the North-west is now on a pretty thoroughly established basis so far as the successful manufacture of butter is concerned. Unfortunately a good many of these creameries required a considerable investment in which the government took a share at the time they were started, and they have not altogether paid off this investment, although some of them have made substantial progress in that direction. I have here a full statement of the accounts of each creamery, but I do not suppose the committee requires all the details. I may say that altogether there were about $48,900 paid out by the government in the shape of loans to these twenty creameries, although some fifteen or sixteen of these creameries have skimming stations attached to them. There was nothing advanced in 1900. The money has been advanced to the patrons to pay them for their milk supplied to the creameries, and is to be recouped when the butter is sold.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: But the management was not to extend until doomsday, it was to end in three years. Is the hon. gentleman stiii carrying them on ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: All of them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That is not keeping good faith with the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is quite right. When we took up this work it was hoped these creameries would be put on a firm basis and be able to carry on the work themselves in three years, but the department as a matter of fact has been obliged to go further.
I grant the hon. gentleman that the expectation was that they would have repaid this money more rapidly than they did. Some of them have done all that was expected of them ; in other eases the creameries have not had as much patronage as was hoped and they are still in debt. In some places the people have begged the department to carry on the management of the work a little longer, and in the interest of the development of the country, and in order to ensure the success of these creameries, the department has thought wise to carry it on still further. I may point out that out of the $46,000 advanced, some $23,000 has been repaid up to the present time. Some of them have practically paid the whole. I may mention a few. The creamery at Calgary received $3,300 and it is owing only $105. Another at Cardston owes $27 ; another at Grenville, which received $2,450, now owes $273. One at Churchbridge was advanced $2,200 and still owes $1,000. The amount of butter made this last year was
637,000	pounds.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
When the hon. gentleman asked for a vote to help these creameries there was no exception taken; but it was pointed out just what would happen, namely, the position in which the hon. gentleman finds himself now. At the same rate it will take ten years more to get these advances recouped. He gave a statement to the House last year. Calgary was in the same position that it is now. Churchbridge. which received an advance of $2,233, has only paid $G13. At this stage it may be well to have some explanation regarding a note for $600 that was given and discounted by the department. I see in the Auditor General's Report, D-75, this is what the Auditor General says in regard to it :
Audit Office, Ottawa, May 11, 1900.
Sir,-Referring to your letter of January 29, relative to a payment of $600 to the Churchbridge Creamery Association as a loan on the security of a note of the directors payable sixteen months after June 2jl, 1898, which note was discounted by your department at the end of the fiscal year, and the proceeds ($592.10) deposited as a refund to the vote from which the payment was made, with the statement in your letter of the date referred to, that the Churchbridge Creamery Association had been asked to refund the amount of the discount, $7.90, I notice that the note in question was taken up by your department by a payment out of this year's vote, cheque No. 19,496, for $600. Please explain why the makers . of the note did not meet their obligation, and

what steps have been taken by you to obtain a repayment of this money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Well, the hon. gentleman, I think, has a pretty full explanation there. As a matter of fact these people were struggling, they were in difficulties and had not the money. We gave them an advance for which the directors of the creamery gave us their Individual and joint note. They have not paid it yet, but they have promised that it will be paid this year. They have been making a lot of butter, and they are progressing. Although they have not been able to pay this note, they have paid $1,250 of the advance made to them, which originally was $2,280, and this $600 besides. Now, they owe $1,013 and the $600.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman last year failed to inform us that he had to pay this $600 out of the vote which he had no authority to do. The hon. gentleman took no vote for that purpose, and he, therefore. had no right to pay the money. However, I am not going to detain the committee upon that point. We will take other cases. The sum advanced for the factory at Innisfail was $6,000, and only $2,000 has been paid; Maple Creek, advanced $1,600, paid $400; Moosejaw, advanced $1,700, paid $1,600; Moosomin, advanced $2,000, paid $700; Prince Albert, advanced $3,100; paid $187; Qu'Appelle, advanced $2,100, paid $700; Red Deer, advanced $700, paid $51 ; Regina, advanced $1,174. paid $1,001 : Saltcoats, advanced $600, paid $150; Emerson, which seems to have had some outlying stations in connection with it, advanced $5,600, paid $600. I shall not continue the list, but I am going to ask the hon. gentleman if there are not some of these factories that he does not expect to pay at all?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The list which the hon. gtntleman has read is no doubt the statement that was given here last year, and it would represent the state of matters at that time. The statement I have now, is the statement of the accounts up to the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Have they altered a great deal ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: They have paid off $3,500 since last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: And there is how much due ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The amount due is $22,000 ; last year it was nearly $26,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Are all the factories to which advances were made in operation ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
There is one which is not. One has been
discontinued because the people in that district have gone into wheat so largely that there are not cows enough to keep it up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: What factory is that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: At Wolseley.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: They received $3,000, and have only paid $600 back. Does the hon. gentleman intend to run these factories until he gets all the money out of them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I trust we will be able to get the money out of them without any difficulty.
Census, $250,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Before that item passes, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if he can lay on the Table of the House a copy of the instructions that are given to the census enumerators together with the form of oath to be taken by them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wishes I can lay a copy of them on the Table at once. I have just sent for them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
There has lately appeared in the public prints, not only in the province of Quebec, but of the province of Ontario a very remarkable circular which has been entrusted to these different enumerators. I may at the outset read it. It has an endorsement which reads as follows, and this circular bears all the imprint of being an official document. The endorsement is as follows :-
Dominion of Canada.
Province of Ontario.

That is the endorsation on the back. The circular form has the following head line:

May X ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if these forms were supplied by his department to the census enumerators to be in turn handed to the sub-enumerators, or if he has any knowledge by whom they were issued ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has referred to a circular which is one I saw published in the Mail and Empire either on Saturday or this morning-I forget in which paper it was. I may say that the document did not emanate in any shape or way from the Department of Agriculture over which I have the honour to preside, and until I saw it in the newspaper I knew nothing about it. I never heard anything about it or knew anything in connection with it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister, since its appearance, has he notified the enumerators that they must disregard this or any such document ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: As I only saw the thing this afternoon, I have not had an opportunity of doing so, but certainly I shall issue instructions to the enumerators employed on the work to ignore any such schedule or circular in connection with their work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
It is rather odd that the hon. minister has only seen this matter to-jday or had his attention called to it. I notice that for several days past it has been coming in for condemnation at the hands of the public press, not only the Conservative press, but also the press of the Liberal side, the Montreal Witness, a newspaper which gives adherence to hon. gentlemen opposite, has been singularly strong in its condemnation of it. A glance- at the document shows that it was issued in an official style from its very make up. The manner in which it was arranged goes to show that there is no doubt as to the reason why, in Ontario particularly, it has been entrusted to the enumerators. On the very face of it, it is plain why these circulars have been issued. In the first place, these enumerators, going about as they are through the country, obtaining the evidence that they are obtaining from parties, are in the best possible position to know who are between the ages of 16 and 21, and they will have the basis ; the net-work for the form of the list in the province of Ontario for the next local election. The endorsement on the back of the document states that these circulars are to be handed to the enumera-Mr. BENNETT.
tors, because it says to the two gentlemen in the subdivision, meaning thereby the enumerators who are to be appointed. It is clear, as I before said, that the whole game was to have these enumerators return to the provincial candidates, or the present member, or the defeated candidate for the Ross government, in Ontario, this information. The result is that they would be fortified by this information, which is almost indispensable to a political party, and they would have it done at the expense of the public treasury of Canada. That is a fraud on the treasury. It is a week ago since Mr. Whitney brought this matter to the attention of the Ontario legislature, and a few days ago the Montreal Witness said :
Mr. Ross was surely very unhappy in his treatment of this matter. Surely it is of some importance to a government that not its party, we hope, but some injudicious member of it, should be guilty of trying to persuade or tempt the census enumerators to perjure themselves, and surely if some of the enumerators who were strong party men were tempted to do so the result would he deplorable. Moreover, such a project on the part of one of the great parties or any considerable section of them, to make use of census information for party purposes, would be just the thing to confirm the dislike and distrust citizens have of giving information to census enumerators, which are already strong enough. It may have been intended by those who issued the circular that the census enumerators should obtain the information asked for separately from the census enumeration, but is it probable that they would inform the citizens that the particulars asked for were not for the census, but for the use of a political party, and thus confess the impertinence of the questions and their own impudence in asking them? If a government treats such affairs as this one as matters of no consequence, it is certainly losing its moral perception and will soon forfeit the confidence of right-thinking people.
It is strange that the minister has not heard of it before this late date. No one will believe that this document in its official form was got up by any single individual on his own responsibility, because it bears on the face of it the evidence that It was fathered by the Liberal political organization. It is the duty of the government to investigate to the bottom as to who has been guilty of [DOT]this fraud on the public treasury. The minister has seen, no doubt, the statement made by Mr. Ross in the provincial legislature, and noticed the flippant manner in which he treated this very grave matter. If the minister (Hon. Mr. Fisher) will refer to the statute, he will find that the enumerators *-.are sworn to do a certain duty, and yet in face of the fact that they are sworn to keep secret the information they get, some of the enumerators, as we have proof, are deliberately violating their oaths. The country will demand that the minister shall investigate this matter at once. The country will demand that this government shall not laugh the matter out of court, as Mr. Ross has attempted. It would be unfair

to charge the government or any member of the government with this fraud, until it is brought home to them, but I believe that if the matter is thoroughly investigated it will be found that the provincial organization of the Liberal party is at the bottom of this wrong-doing. The government have the Dominion police force under its control, and they have ample means of finding out who supplied the enumerators with this document. The country will demand that the Minister of Agriculture shall have his chief enumerators placed on the stand under oath to declare who supplied these documents. A thorough investigation of that kind is the only means by which the government can clear itself. If they fail in this, the ministers will bring down on themselves the utter contempt of the people for such conduct. Even their own party organs to-day have condemned the tiling. The law declares that these enumerators must not exact any further information than is on the schedule. It clearly says in section 11 : * And no other such information.' Is there anything to be found in the schedule about asking a man what his politics are ? Not at all. Whoever was at the bottom of this fraud had not only in mind the obtaining of an advantage for the local government, but they are asked to make inquiries of men between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one, so it is plainly intended that when the next Federal elections come on, the Liberal party in the Dominion should have a knowledge of the politics of the men who shall then be twenty-one, so as to help them in the preparation of their lists. In the famous circular issued by Mr. Cote, chief commissioner for the province of Quebec, he states that all this information is obtained under oath, and as I have not yet seen the form of tlie oath, I shall reserve my remarks on that point until later. I do trust that the Minister of Agriculture will rise in liis place to-night and announce that he will institute a thorough investigation in order to please his friend, the Montreal Witness, and in order to give Liberals as well as Conservatives throughout the country an assurance that the perpetrators of this gross fraud shall be discovered and punished. This government is fond of commissions. Let it produce its enumerators before a competent commission, and let it discover who is guilty of this infamous act. Surely, there must be some law in this country to punish the men who are caught red-handed perpetrating this fraud.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I have stated already, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) no doubt accepts my statement, as I am sure the committee will, that I knew nothing whatever about this matter until it was drawn to my attention to-day in a copy of the Mail and Empire. I did not look to see what was the date of the copy, but I think it was the issue of last Saturday. I knew nothing whatever, and
I have not heard anything except what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has said, in regard to the debate in the Toronto legislature. I have not followed the proceedings there. I did not know the question was up there, and I did not see either Mr. Whitney's or Mr. Ross' statement in regard to it. 'To-day for the first time the matter was brought to my attention. I have stated, and I state again, that if anything has been done beyond the law and the requirements of the duties of the enumerators, they will be brought to task, and it will be seen by me as head of the department under which they are working, that they do their work legally, lawfully, and properly, according to the strict letter of the law which lays down their duties. If any of them do anything which is wrong and improper, they will be brought to book and prevented doing it in the future. As regards investigation,
I will find out the facts of this matter, and will be guided by the facts I discover in my departmental search and inquiry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I have made some inquiries in regard to this matter, and I am informed by a member of the Ontario legislature that it was practically admitted in the debate there, that these forms had been supplied to the census enumerators.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
By whom ?
Mr.- BORDEN (Halifax). I do not know.
I am not charging the hon. gentleman. It does not make any difference by whom. It has been done by some person, and if this * circular which has been sent out by the hon. gentleman's department and for which he assumes responsibility, the circular signed by Mr. Cot6, if that is correct, then whoever put this into the hands of the census enumerators was asking the census enumerators to commit perjury. The circular sent out by Mr. Cote declares that the enumerators are sworn to secrecy. Any census enumerator who undertook to supply the information asked for in this political memorandum which the member for Simcoe has brought to the attention of the House should instantly be dismissed from the position. Any census enumerator who undertook to act upon it without reporting to the hon. gentleman's department with respect to it, is unworthy to hold his position. Not only has the enumerator been asked to commit perjury, but he has been asked to defraud the government, for this reason, that every one of these men is paid by the day, and he is expected to have these circulars filled out during the time for which he is paid by the government. The result is that whoever has put these circulars into the hands of the census enumerators for the purpose of having them filled out, and then sent to Liberal members or to unsuccessful Liberal candidates at the last election, is asking that those enumerators shall commit perjury and also commit fraud on this

government. Therefore, X am surprised that the hou. gentleman should hesitate about an investigation. I think this is one of the most disgraceful attempts ever heard of in this country. If anything is worthy of an Investigation, it is a transaction of this kind, in which, so far as the facts are before us, certain gentlemen belonging to a political party, have not only sought to violate the law which these census enumerators are sworn to preserve, but have also sought to have performed by them at the expense of the country, certain work which should be done by any political organization at its own expense. I therefore sincerely trust that the hon. gentleman will see fit to make the investigation necessary to get at the real facts of this matter, and will see that any person who has attempted to commit an act of that kind shall be brought to justice and punished so far as the laws of this country are able to punish him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. minister where the form of oath js to be found in the instructions ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I do not think the form of oath is in the instructions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if the issue of CotS's circular received the endorsement of the department ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I would like first to reply to the leader of the opposition. The hon. gentleman must have misinterpreted what I said, if he thought that I was desirous in any wTay of shielding anybody or preventing an investigation. The facts were only to-day brought to my notice in the form of a newspaper article. I purpose to find out exactly what the facts are, so far as I can, and to be guided by what I find as to the future action. I am not prepared to say what chat action will be until I have investigated the facts ; nor am I prepared to take a newspaper article as a necessarily accurate statement of the facts. When my own departmental investigation shows me what the facts are, I shall be able to state exactly to the House what 1 will do in connection therewith. I do not think the committee would expect me to do more than that. I am quite prepared to say that anybody connected with the census who has contravened the law or gone beyond his instructions shall be dealt with in the way in which any man who does wrong should be dealt with. Replying to the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) with regard to the Cot6 circular, as he calls it, I may say that the letter signed by Mr. Cote and sent out, with regard to the way in which certain enumerations should be taken, meets with the approval of myself as the head of the department. I see nothing in that letter that is in any Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
way objectionable. It was written and issued to the enumerators for the purpose of securing an accurate enumeration of the people, and as such it meets writh the approval of the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I might say to the hon. gentleman that these facts were brought to the attention of the public as far back as Thursday last; and although I did not take any action in regard to the matter until Saturday, I procured one of the original circulars sent to the census enumerators, and I have it in my possession now. I might also point out that the handing of these circulars to these men was apparently done in a very insidious way, and done to deceive the public and make them believe that it was necessary for them to answer the questions there asked, because section 22 of the Census Act states that any form purporting to be an authorized form is prima facie evidence that it is the proper form. Apart from any such provision of the statute, a form printed in this way, with all the appearance of verisimilitude, would be apt to deceive nine out of every ten people with the idea that it was something the government was actually asking them to fill in,
* Mr. INGRAM. It is well known, I think, to all the public men in Canada, that some such movement as the issue of this circular was contemplated some months ago ; and if the government believed such an idea was a good one, why did they not issue the circular in the ordinary way and take the full responsibility of it the same as any other document connected with the census ? The hon. gentleman stated to-day that 744 of these circulars were sent to Ontario, 19(5 to New Brunswick, 287 to Prince Edward Island and 441 to British Columbia, or a total of 1,855. If these figures are correct, they only amount to 1,668, so that there is a discrepancy as to the number sent out. I have only to say that if it goes throughout the country that this assistant census commissioner issued this circular, that is one reason to my mind why such a circular as that read by the hon. member for East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett) has been circulated throughout a portion of the province of Ontario. It seems to me it is a bad way to commence the work of taking the census The document should have been officially issued by the government. If that had been done, we would not have heard the criticism we have heard to-night. For my part, I do not think the government can be condemned too strongly. So far as the Prime Minister of Ontario is concerned, when his attention was drawn to this circular he made light of it as a very trifling affair. I can easily understand that. The Prime Minister of Ontario has so far forgotten his duty as an honourable man in conducting the affairs of the province that it would require a great

deal to prick his conscience. He is lost to all sense of honour, and therefore he treated the matter in the light way he did. But I think the time is not far distant when a man with a greater sense of honour will control the province of Ontario, and then we shall hear no more of such transactions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Is the form of oath required in section 14 on the file ? It says that a form of oath shall he furnished to the enumerators which shall be contained in an order in council, and I cannot find it in the papers at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The form of oath was sent to the enumerators, but it is not in this book of instructions. It was a separate paper.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Is there not one available for the House ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I can get one from the department and lay it on the Table. It was inadvertently omitted from these papers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said he approved of what he called the Cote circular. Did he sanction it as an official document before it was issued ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I authorized Mr. Cote to write such a letter. I did not see that particular letter before it was sent out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether he directed the assistant commissioner to put ' confidential' on an official document ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I said a moment ago that I did not see that particular document before it went out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that he authorized such a document. I ask him if he authorized this paid agent of the Canadian government to write a confidential circular to certain people ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: No, I did not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Then the minister did not carefully consider this matter, which is creating a great deal of feeling throughout the country, and he was not correct in saying that he authorized that document ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I said I authorized Mr. Cote to write a letter, but I did not authorize the words of that particular letter, because I did not see it before it was sent out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
It seems to me that the bon. gentleman ought not to allow a letter of that kind to be sent out without first revising it. I have some knowledge of the taking of censuses, and I have yet to learn
that it has ever been considered necessary that the man next the commissioner should send out a confidential circular to any part of the population. What makes this more grave is, that it will convince people that the information which they are assured will be kept secret may at any time become public property, and, at any rate, it is to be put into the hands of the machine politicians. It is evident that these machine men, who run the elections for hon. gentlemen opposite, are to be given every access to the information taken by the census commissioner, and every facility for utilizing it in the interests of their employers. I have never heard of anything of the kind having been done in this or any other British country, nor has it ever been resorted to in-the neighbouring republic, and I know something of the method of taking the census in that country. I hope that for the sake of the good name of the government and of parliament and of the country, this matter will be thoroughly investigated. If we cannot have this investigation made by the enumerators, let the government employ the police and the detectives who are paid by this country, and let the men who sent out these circulars be punished with the extreme penalty of the law.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
The hon. the Minister of Agriculture has said that he approves entirely of the circular sent out by Mr. Cote to the French Canadians, and marked ' confidential.' I am glad to say, that although the minister approves of this circular, there are some men to whom it was sent who do not. I received a letter some days ago from a French Canadian who lives in British Columbia, and to whom this French circular was sent. He wrote me as follows :
107 Moss Street, Victoria, B.C.,
March 21, 1901.
Col. Prior, M.P.
Dear Sir,-Inclosed please find a communication that was sent to me, and a_copy of my reply thereto.
They will speak for themselves, and I hope you will bring the matter forward and have it threshed out, that we may know who is responsible.
I would feel obliged if you would return me the circular when you are done with it.
Believe me, yours truly,
T. A. LePAGE.
The letter which he inclosed reads as follows :
107 Moss Street, Victoria, B.C.,
March 21, 1901.
Thomas Cote, Esq.,
Assistant Census Commissioner.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your printed ciruciar, dated March 1, 1901.
Whilst I shall be pleased to do all that lies in my power to assist the census commissioners in their laudable endeavours to get a true and correct census in every detail, still I must say that it is with considerable regret that I find there is an evident deliberate intention on the

part of some in authority to foster and keep alive racial feelings and prejudices (I will not say hatreds) between the French and English population of Canada.
To me their duty lies clearly the other way- to smooth over and obliterate all traces of the unhappy relations of the two races on Canadian soil in the centuries that are gone, and in teaching the written history of the past to the young of both races, to impress upon them that as it was their duty and glory in the days gone by to stand foot to foot, so now it must be equally their pride and pleasure to march forward towards the universal brotherhood of all men.
I am sending your communication to me, with a copy of my reply, to Col. Prior, M.P., one of our members of the House of Commons, with a request to him to endeavour to find out from his place in parliament if it is with the knowledge and consent of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government, that this unwise and unpatriotic policy is being pursued.
I remain, sir,
Your humble servant,
T. A. LePAGE.
P.S.-L'union c'est la force.
That is the opinion of a French Canadian who lives in British Columbia, and to whom this French circular was sent. Why was that circular marked ' confidential ' ? I do not know by whom it was franked, but the circular was marked ' confidential.' Had Mr. Cfitfi instructions from the bon. gentleman to make it confidential. Ottawa, April 1st, 1901.
Hon. Col. Prior, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
Dear Col. Prior,-I have received from one of your electors, Mr. T. A. LePage, on March the 21st, a communication of which you have also received a copy. As you have received from Mr. LePage said communication, I beg- to inclose you a copy of my answer, which will, I think, demonstrate to you that there was no intention whatever on my part to ' foster and keep alive racial feelings and prejudices between the French and English population of Canada.'
Truly yours,
THOMAS COTE, Assistant Census Commissioner.
April 1st, 1901.
T. A. LePage, Esq.,
107 Moss Street, Victoria, B.C.
Dear Sir,-I have received your communication of March the 21st. I am sorry that you did not understand the meaning of my letter of the 1st ultimo. If I am to judge by the last sentence of your letter, you are able to read and speak the French language. Perhaps, though, I am mistaken. In case I am, I beg to send you herewith a verbatim translation of my first communication to you. In reading it over carefully, I think that you shall come to the conclusion that you have no justification whatever in finding that ' there is an evident deliberate intention on the part of some one Mr. PRIOR.
in authority to foster and keep alive racial feelings and prejudices between the French and English population of Canada.'
You are, yourself, evidently from French origin. Would you tell me in what way you will be hurting the feelings of your fellow-countrymen of English origin in having your own origin properly registered in the census tables?
In the province of Quebec, the two elements of population are living in harmony; but, in the meantime, both of them are proud of their origin. The English people keep their traditions as the French do for their own. This, by any means, does not prevent them from being good citizens of this country and of working hand-to-hand for its prosperity.
In looking carefully into the census tables, you will find that I have not written you one word which was not justifiable and right. On table No. 1 there is a column for the origin, a column for the mother tongue when spoken, and also a column for the nationality, which must be, and in fact is, for every citizen of Canada, ' Canadian.- This will demonstrate to you that the census will be taken, this year, in such a way that the German, or English, or French, or Scotch, or Irish, origin of a man will be ascertained. If a man like you see fit to declare to the census-taker that he is from English origin, when in fact he is from French origin, that is his own business.
In our province, we have persons by the name of Ross, of MacLean, of Warren, of Carroll, &c., who are evidently from Irish, Scotch or English origin. Many of them don't speak any more the English language. They do speak French. In the census tables they will be registered as being from Irish, Scotch or English origin, as the case may be, and in the column of the language they will be registered as speaking the French language.
Why, I want to know, a citizen of French origin living in British Columbia, or in other English provinces, and speaking no more the French language, should not be registered in the column of the origins as being from French origin, and in the column of the language as speaking the English language? Where do you see in that any attempt to ' foster and keep alive racial feelings and prejudices between the French and English population of Canada?
Candidly, I think you have not understood the question at all.
I deny altogether the charge that you have made. There was not and there is not any intention on my part to keep alive what you call ' racial feelings and prejudices.' I have the pretension of being too good a Canadian for that, and I think that I do understand better than you do, that It is possible in this country to be proud of our ancestors and of our origin, and, in the meantime, to live in peace and In harmony with every one.
Truly yours,

A particular number of citizens were selected to send this circular to, and it was to be a confidential circular. Why was not the rest of the population to know anything about this circular which was sent out ? Its contents were not to be divulged because it was marked ' confidential.' He says that he was unaware of it until it was sent out and published, but that he has since seen it, and that he heartily endorses it. (Mr. Prior), was, I presume, born in England, and when he puts his name down as being of English birth, he cannot claim to be a native Canadian as well. Mr. Whitney sprang a surprise by producing a copy of a circular which has been sent out in thousands to census enumerators all over the province, directing them to fill out certain forms stating the politics and religion of every male over sixteen in their ridings, and forward this record to the Liberal member or defeated candidate in the riding. This information, it was proposed to use, said Mr. Whitney, in the coming Ontario and the next Dominion general elections.
Mr. Whitney pointed out that as census enumerators were sworn to secrecy, this was a direct inducement, almost a command, to them to perjure themselves. The moment they complied with the request they would be guilty of perjury.

Mr. Fisher) in reference to which every paper in Canada was ringing about on Friday morning; a thing that every person in Canada except the Minister of Agriculture knew all about, and he was oblivious and ignorant of the whole thing until this Monday morning. The Hon. Mr. Ross, the premier, in response, admitted that the Liberal party had fathered the circulars, and made light of the matter. It did not appear a conspiracy against the public weal in his eyes.
Mr. Ross admitted that the Liberal party had fathered this circular. Who is the Liberal party and where are the headquarters of the Liberal party, and who directs its movements. Is it the right hon. the leader of the Uominion government ? He is the head of the Liberal party in this Dominion. Is he the father of the circular 7 I shall not accuse him of it, because I do not believe he would be guilty of conduct like that. I will freely exonerate him from any such conduct. But Mr. Ross, the Prime Minister of Ontario, says that the Liberal party fathered the responsibility of the circular, and as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) has pointed out, that circular is a conspiracy against the nation. And, Sir, any enumerator who attempts to carry out the instructions of that circular can be arrested and will be arrested for perjury. It was the duty of the Minister of Agriculture on Friday morning last to telegraph to every one in charge of a census district and threaten them with all the penalties of the law if they did not at once destroy that infamous circular. A minister placed in charge of responsible duties as the head of a department cannot shirk his responsibility by saying that he knew nothing about this.
What are the objects of it 7 To furnish at the expense of the people of Canada information for the benefit of a political party -information which they have no right to ask from the people. The man who goes to the head of a household and asks for the information referred to in this circular has been instructed by whom 7 By the Liberal party. Where did the Liberal party get authority any more than the Conservative party to send such a circular to every census enumerator 7 The authority comes through this parliament of Canada, and nowhere else ; and if any other authority attempts to thrust itself on these enumerators, the government of this country should arrest the perpetrators and put them in the common jail, and try them for high crimes and misdemeanours. The premier of Ontario has committed the Liberal party to these circulars, for he admitted that the Liberal party had fathered them. He could not get out of it. It would not do to repeat the old story that the ballots were burnt in the cellar of the legislature of Ontario, and that they took fire by spontaneous combustion. That kind of yarn did not go down in that case, and it will not in this. This circular was printed at somebody's expense, and we presume it was handed to every census enumerator in Ontario, and the Minister of Agriculture folds his arms utterly uncon-

cerned about it, saying that he will consider it, that be did not bear of it until to-day, and be does not propose to do anything even at this late hour of the day. fifteen days elapsed before be knew anything about it. That circular must have reached the census enumerators before they started on their duties on the 1st of April. A nice way the business is being conducted. In the meantime the census enumerators have been filling up these circulars. One of them goes to a man, we will assume, and asks the date of his birth, the number of the lot or house

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: So long as he does not go to the graveyards to get information, as you did in 1891, it will be all right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Saskatchewan had better get another haul of half-breed scrip, and it will satisfy him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: We will have to give you a scrip.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The enumerator will also get the nationality, the post office address, the religion, and the church to which the man belongs ; and then he has to make some remarks. He will also get the man's politics. What right have these enumerators to go to a household and ask the politics of any man in this country ? Who gave them authority to do that ? As the hon. member for East Simcoe pointed out, if a citizen having a schedule placed before him refuses to answer the questions in it, he can be prosecuted. When asked what his politics are, his natural inclination would be to say : It is nobody's business what my politics are ; I can disclose them, or I can refuse to disclose them, just as I please.' I would like to know where in all this country it is permitted to ask a man what his politics are. We have voting by ballot in this country, and it is supposed to be secret and sacred. But here is something put down in front of you, and it is said that there are severe pains and penalties if you refuse to answer anything in that circular. What right has the Minister of Agriculture to countenance the promulgation of that circular ? He says he did not know anything about it until to-day. What has he done since he did know about it ? Has he done anything ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Will the hon. member for West York allow me to ask him a question ? Will he tell us what proof there is that that particular circular which he is alluding to was sent to the census enumerators ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I will tell him why :
Mr. Whitney sprung a surprise by producing a copy of a circular which had been sent out by thousands to census enumerators all over the province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: You are reading from a newspaper article. I will admit they are not always reliable.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I am not reading a newspaper article in that sense. I am reading a report of a debate in the local legislature.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That still is no proof of your statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I will give the answer which the hon. member for West Huron wants :
The premier, in response, admitted that the Liberal party had fathered these circulars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The hon. member for West York has not answered my question still. There is no proof in the statement, or the.article you are quoting from, that the circular was sent to a census enumerator. It is only a matter of assumption.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I would like to know if the hon. gentleman will accept the confession of the premier of Ontario ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The premier of Ontario does not say so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The premier of Ontario said distinctly that the Liberal party had fathered these circulars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That does not say that it was sent to the census enumerators.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: You will not deny it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I do< deny it as far as I know anything about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had known what took place, in the Ontario parliament, he would not have asked the question he did. It was distinctly argued there that the form of this circular showed that it was intended to be placed in the hands of the census enumerators ; the whole make-up of it showed that, and when the debate took place in the Ontario parliament, that was not denied.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: With all deference to the hon. leader of the opposition, I take exception to his statement. If that circular was sent to the census enumerators, I ask for the proof. All this argument is based on assumption, pure and simple.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The assumption is all on the side of the hon. member for West Huron. We have the evidence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: You have no proof of it at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: We have the statement made by Mr, Whitney in the local legislature, and the admission of Mr. Ross.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Mr. Whitney does not state that it was sent to the census enumerators. I challenge the hon. member for West York to show that he did.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I will accept tlie challenge :
Mr. Whitney sprung a surprise by producing a copy of a circular which had been sent out by thousands to census enumerators all over the province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I admit that, hut I do not accept that as proof.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Then I am only wasting valuable time discussing the matter any further with our good friend from West Huron. Mr. Whitney makes the statement distinct and positive, and Mr. Ross admits the truth of it, and says it is only a trifling matter not worth bothering about. Yet the hon. gentleman, census commissioner and assistant commissioners, and all that great staff of diligent officials which we read about-not one of them is able to tell the Minister of Agriculture a word about it, and he tells us that he is in utter ignorance of the fact. Does the hon. gentleman intend doing anything ? The hon. gentleman pleads that he does not read the newspapers, but [DOT] he should read them and inform himself and see that the guilty are prosecuted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: We should have some information laid on the Table with regard to the instructions and circulars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I laid the instructions and schedules on the Table a few minutes ago.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: What about this special circular ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That was not sent to the enumerators at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That circular was sent out, and we want it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I have nothing to do with that and know nothing about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I understood that a certain circular referred to by the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) would be laid on the Table.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I know nothing of such a circular, but if there is any such I shall only be too happy to lay it on the Table.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I also understood that certain instructions, to which the hon. gentleman referred in the afternoon, would be laid on the Table.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Yes, the instructions sent to enumerators in the province of Quebec, which are referred to in Mr. Cote's letter, will be laid on the Table also.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Better let the item stand until these are laid on the Table.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
Why not pass the item ? We have only
passed two items so far although we have been at work four hours.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: They were very important items.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Are there any instructions other than those in the book I have in my hand, and which was laid on the Table, given to the enumerators ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Not that I know of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I shall not speak for any riding outside my own, but taking the intelligence of some of the enumerators in that riding, they will have considerable trouble wrestling with some of these instructions. [ He is one of them :
In every case where members of the family or household are temporarily absent from their home or usual place of abode, their names or records should be dealt with so as to conform, as near as may be, with the general conception of a de jure system of enumeration.
Can the hon. minister inform the House what is the general conception of a de jure system of enumeration ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Now that the minister has seen the circular sent to the enumerators, to which Mr. Whitney refers, and which the Prime Minister of Ontario admitted was sent to him he should be able to give us some information as to the action he has taken to bring this matter to the attention of the enumerators throughout Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: And what has been done with these circulars by the census enumerators ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to explain for the benefit of the enumerators, what he means by that clause in the instructions in which he tells the enumerators to conform, in the case of those who are temporarily absent, as nearly as may be with the general conception of a de jure system of enumeration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: There are two well known systems of taking the census-one the de jure and the other de facto. In the de facto census, nobody is entered except those actually present at the date of taking the census. But under the de jure system, people temporarily absent are counted as being in the place from which they were absent at the moment, but which is their usual residence and home. In this way, people are taken who are not present when the questions of the census are put. I do not know that there is any legal definition of the word de jure. No doubt, the hon. gentleman knows the exact meaning of it, but this is what I may call a technical definition of the de jure census as distinguished from a de facto census.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
The words occur a few lines above ' temporarily absent.' Are they

expected to enumerate persons who may be temporarily absent, in the United States, for instance, and is there any schedule for such absentees ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The people who are absent from their homes, when they are in another part of this country or beyond it's borders are, by a de jure census, counted, provided the absence is not greater than a year. Or, if the people there state positively that the person is only absent temporarily, and has not made his home elsewhere he is counted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Can the hon. minister show where the instructions are restricted to a year's absence ? I do not find it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
I icannot find It at the moment, but it is there, I know.
Quarantine-Salaries and contingencies of organized districts and public health in other districts, $f0,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: There is an increase here of $5,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: That is due partly to increased work in connection with the protections of our frontier between the United States and ourselves. There has been a great deal of small-pox in the United States, and some little in Canada, and the people along the border have demanded that we should protect them against the bringing in of disease. I might say that I shall have to ask a further amount in the supplementary estimates, because the work is increasing. It is partly due also to the precautions against the bubonic plague which has caused us to make expenditures in connection with people coming in from the Orient.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: What description of protection has the hon. gentleman adopted with regard to the small-pox and the bubonic plague ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: We have required the fumigation and cleansing of all oriental incomers. Ordinarily, unless disease is aetualy found we allow them to pass, but the inspection now is more strict. This causes a great increase of work at the William's Head station. We have also to examine vessels coming coastwise from the United States ports which formerly came in without examination. As to the small-pox, we have named officers along the frontier whose duty it is to enforce vaccination upon people coming in from districts in the United States where there is small-pox. This involves heavy expenditure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Is that carried on all along the frontier or only on a portion of it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Wherever there seems to be danger. The chief superintendent general of public health is in constant touch with United States authorities, and learns just where the danger of small-pox is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
As there is to be another vote for quarantine, the subject can be further discussed.
Quarantine-Cattle quarantine, $35,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: There is an increase here of $3,500 as compared with last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
That is due to work In North-west Territories. The work formerly was done by the mounted police. But, in consequence of the South African war, veterinary surgeons and others trained to the work have been called away. They have not returned and we have had to engage outside workers, besides making a new arrangement with the mounted police officers, giving them a little more, because the work has increased throughout the Territories.
Quarantine-Compensation for slaughter of hogs and sheep and all other expenses connected therewith, $10,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: What is the meaning of that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: This service has been carried on for a long time, in the province of Ontario especially, but not exclusive. It is designed to protect against disease among hogs known as hog cholera. We have been pretty successful in stamping it out of late. We are asking $5,000 less this year than last. We were not called upon to use all the vote of last year, and we believe that $10,000 will be sufficient.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Does the Ontario government contribute to this ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
Not that I am aware of.
Quarantine-Towards the prevention of the spread of tuberculosis in cattle throughout the Dominion, $25,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I may say that the demand for tests with tuberculine is largely increasing. The people are gaining confidence from year to year in this test. But I have been obliged to increase the number of officers in consequence of certain action of the American authorities, who, heretofore, have accepted the certificates of our veterinary officers, but have now passed a regulation under which they will only accept certificates of the permanent officers of the department. I am making arrangements by which slightly to increase the number of permanent officers, and expect these officers to take complete charge of all this work, instead of -rjbarging

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: fees, as was done to a certain extent before.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: In the arrangements made with the United States authorities, is there a provision that animals going from Canada to be slaughtered must have a certificate of good health to accompany them ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext:
It is only animals for breeding and dairy purposes that require these certificates, animals for slaughter do not.
Some resolutions reported.
The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: Will the right hon. gentleman state what will be taken up to-morrow ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: If the Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) is here, as I hope he will be, we will take up the Election Bill ; if not, one or two of the Bills of the Minister of the Interior, and then go into Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture says he will not proceed with the census items, so we will take up either Public Works or Interior.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

maintopic: SUPPLY-PENSIONS TO HEADQUARTERS STAFF, PERMANENT MILITIA.
speechtext: I shall require time to get some information to lay on the Table.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Tuesday.
Tuesday, April 16, 1901.
